newsletters.title: When Trying to Make AI Better Makes It Worse
newsletters.content:
A million words of failed drafts taught me that improving my AI setup sometimes means giving it fewer rules to follow  ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌

WHEN TRYING TO MAKE AI BETTER MAKES IT WORSE https://every.?ev_audience=free


A MILLION WORDS OF FAILED DRAFTS TAUGHT ME THAT IMPROVING MY AI SETUP SOMETIMES MEANS GIVING IT FEWER RULES TO FOLLOW https://every.?ev_audience=free

by Katie Parrott https://every.?ev_audience=free

Midjourney/Every illustration.

Was this newsletter forwarded to you? Sign up https://every.?ev_audience=free to get it in your inbox.



----------------------------------------

It is a well-known fact that the Germans have a word for everything. Kummerspeck, literally “grief bacon,” is the weight you put on from emotional eating. Torschlusspanik, “gate-closing panic,” is the fear that time is running out to do the thing you’re supposed to do with your life.



Recently, I came across another gem: Verschlimmbesserung, or “worsen-bettering.” It refers to our desire to make something better, only to make it worse. Used in a sentence: “Ich habe meinen Kontext verschlimmbessert,” or “I have worsen-bettered my context.”

That’s precisely what I did to the context that drives my AI setup over a few weeks in September. By “context,” I’m referring to the style guides, examples, and instructions that tell Claude and ChatGPT who I am, how I write, and what I’m working on. When my context is good, my AI “assistants” can find what they need to do work the way I want them to do it—including writing essay drafts https://every.?ev_audience=free the way I want them written.

But a few weeks ago, my context went bad, and so did my work. Drafts came back crowded and flat. When I told the model what was wrong, the next draft came back worse. The system I’d built to keep me afloat started pulling me down with it. For a while, I stopped trusting my context. Then I stopped trusting myself.

You don’t need an elaborate setup to run into this problem. You might have asked your AI to keep answers short, then found yourself fighting it for a thorough explanation, or saved a successful draft as an example and watched its quirks turn up in everything that followed. A preference that helps with one task can get in the way of the next, especially when it has to coexist with everything else you’ve ever asked the model to remember.

* Trump just created a “Super Intelligence Force”

* OpenAI is putting ads inside image generation

* Plus trending AI tools, posts, and resources

Let’s _dive_ into the Valley of AI…

#### **DIIO**

## [Move AI from passive observer to active participant](https://www.diio.com/us/starter-diio?utm_source=ai_valley&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=ai_valley_2026&utm_content=2026-10-05&utm_term=main_ad_starter)

AI has become incredibly good at listening. The next step is understanding what to do with what it hears.

That’s what diio is built for.

diio analyzes business conversations across meetings, calls, WhatsApp, and other customer interactions to understand their context, objective, and the signals inside them.

Its AI identifies customer needs, objections, commitments, risks, next steps, and whether a conversation is actually moving toward its intended outcome. It can guide teams against their own playbooks, surface patterns across thousands of interactions, and turn what customers are saying into intelligence teams can act on.

Instead of treating conversations as recordings to summarize later, diio turns them into a live source of business context.

The result is AI becoming an active part of how revenue teams understand customers, improve execution, and decide what happens next.

[Try for free](https://www.diio.com/us/starter-diio?utm_source=ai_valley&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=ai_valley_2026&utm_content=2026-10-05&utm_term=main_ad_starter)

~_*This is sponsored_~


----------

----------
#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/f110954a-f584-4833-88d6-2fd33793a277/Reflection-AI-cofounders-1-scaled__1_.png?t=1791210740)
Caption: Reflection AI Co-Founders Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou

**1/ Reflection is about to drop a big American open-weight AI model** - the Nvidia-backed startup is [reportedly](https://www.axios.com/2026/10/04/reflection-open-weight-ai) preparing to release its first model, aimed squarely at Chinese open models like Kimi and Qwen. It probably won't beat the absolute best models from OpenAI, Anthropic or Google at launch, but Axios says it'll be competitive with the top Chinese open-weight models.

That's actually important because China pretty much dominates the high-end open-weight model market right now. Reflection is trying to build a Western alternative that companies can download, customize and run themselves instead of sending everything through OpenAI or Anthropic's APIs.

But the bigger plan is something Reflection calls an “AI factory.” Basically, give it your company's private data, Reflection's models and a bunch of Nvidia GPUs, and you can build your own proprietary AI system. For companies sitting on really valuable data, like banks, hedge funds or even governments, that's a pretty compelling pitch.

The model is apparently coming soon, alongside several other Western open-weight models this month.

**2/ Trump just created a “Super Intelligence Force”** - [yes](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117382616783706638), that's actually what it's called. After telling the US government to start calling AI “Super Intelligence” last week, Trump has now named Director of National Intelligence [Jay Clayton](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/04/jay-clayton-ai-trump-01106137) as his AI czar and put him in charge of a new White House task force focused on it.

The group has 120 days to study the risks and opportunities of AI and recommend what Washington should actually do about it, including how to handle AI incidents, cyberattacks and advanced models going wrong.

Clayton seems pretty firmly on the acceleration side. He says the risk of America _not_ being first in AI is high and has pushed back on calls to pause development. Basically, figure out how to make this stuff safer without slowing the US down.

And apparently we're really committing to the whole “SI” thing now. [Elon Musk says](https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/musk-says-he-will-rename-spacexai-spacexsi-2026-10-04/) he's renaming SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI.

**3/ OpenAI is putting ads inside image generation** - OpenAI is [testing a new ad format](https://openai.com/index/new-chatgpt-ads-format-and-measurement/) that shows sponsored products and experiences while you're generating images in ChatGPT, starting in the US later this month.

The ads will be labeled and kept separate from your actual content, and OpenAI says advertising still won't influence ChatGPT's answers. But image generation is a pretty interesting place to put them. Ask ChatGPT to design your living room, generate an outfit or visualize a new desk setup, and there are suddenly a lot of products that could naturally be advertised alongside what you're making.

No pricing yet, and OpenAI hasn't announced a way to opt out of these image-generation ads.

* [Kolibri](https://x.com/Aleph__Alpha/status/2106306840657297814?s=20) - 78B parameters. 3.46B active. Up to 1M tokens of context. Built in Europe

* [Grok Bot](https://x.com/bot/status/2105373767568621895) - hand off coding tasks to Cursor, manage PRs with GitHub and Origin plugins

newsletters.content:
Five prompts that took me from one-off chats to delegating whole projects to teams of agents  ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌
https://every.?ev_audience=free


HOW TO GET BETTER AT AI BY ASKING AI https://every.?ev_audience=free


FIVE PROMPTS THAT TOOK ME FROM ONE-OFF CHATS TO DELEGATING WHOLE PROJECTS TO TEAMS OF AGENTS https://every.?ev_audience=free

by Arielle Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free

Midjourney/Every illustration.

Was this newsletter forwarded to you? Sign up https://every.?ev_audience=free to get it in your inbox.



----------------------------------------



For most of my working life, the first step of any task began with a blank slate: an empty Google Doc, a fresh email, or a new Excel spreadsheet. From researching to writing formulas, the banalities of every stage of construction fell to me. AI made that process faster, but the way I accomplished it wasn’t all that different. I started with a new chat and prompted it over and over until the output matched my unspoken definition of “done.”

When I started at Every in May, I was still working that way. When I needed to issue contractor payments, I worked from one chat thread, prompting sequentially to surface agreement terms, approve payment, and send email confirmations that payment had been issued.

Things look very different today. Last week, I needed to verify the cost of purchasing equity for an employee across multiple grants, strike prices, and vesting schedules. Rather than tackle this complex task in a single thread, I split the project among several subagents that coordinated independently to verify information on signed agreements, run the math, double-check it and flag discrepancies, and return a draft of a Slack message that I could approve with a simple “yes.” That work ran on skills, orchestrator threads, context packets, subagents, MCPs, and computer use. It’s a veritable alphabet soup of technical terms that I was previously sure could only be understood and deployed by Highly Technical People, yet I now find myself reaching for these techniques daily, helping me work faster, with better and more precise results that I can be confident about.

I was prompted to make the shift from a tweet. Katie Parrott https://every.?ev_audience=free tweeted https://every.?ev_audience=free in June that she had asked Codex where she fell on Mike Taylor https://every.

* SoftBank now owns ~13% of OpenAI

Let’s _dive_ into the Valley of AI…


----------

----------
#### **DIIO**

## [What if AI understood why a conversation was happening?](https://www.diio.com/us/starter-diio?utm_source=ai_valley&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=ai_valley_2026&utm_content=2026-10-02&utm_term=main_ad_starter)

Caption: Courtesy: Diio

Most AI tools can capture what was said. diio understands what the conversation was trying to accomplish.

diio analyzes customer interactions across meetings, calls, WhatsApp, and other channels, combining the content of the conversation with its context, objective, and your team’s own playbooks.

That lets its AI go beyond summaries. It can identify customer needs, objections, commitments, risks, next steps, and signals that indicate whether an interaction is progressing toward its goal.

The result is a continuously growing intelligence layer built from real conversations — not just notes or structured fields.

Teams can use that intelligence to understand customers, prioritize what needs attention, improve how they execute, and act on signals hidden across thousands of interactions.

diio turns conversations into context AI can understand and context into better decisions.

[Try it for free](https://www.diio.com/us/starter-diio?utm_source=ai_valley&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=ai_valley_2026&utm_content=2026-10-02&utm_term=main_ad_starter)

~_*This is sponsored_~


----------

----------
#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

Youtube: 48% of People Thought This AI Was a Real Human | Introducing Griffin (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lHw6yoyPkpo)

**Tavus built an AI that fooled 48% of people on video calls** - its new [Griffin](https://www.tavus.io/griffin) model can see, hear, talk and react simultaneously during live video calls. Unlike most existing AI video models that take turns speaking, Griffin can watch and listen while it talks. It can nod mid-sentence, handle interruptions, change its facial expressions and even talk about things it sees on your screen.

The result is incredibly convincing. In a study Tavus conducted with 54 people, 48% thought Griffin-Lite was a real human after a one-minute blind video call. Its previous model managed just 2.4%. Griffin also topped NVIDIA's VideoFDB benchmark, scoring 3.83/5 on NVIDIA’s video full-duplex benchmark, compared to 3.92/5 for a real human (that gap is way too small).

While that video call study had a small number of participants and was conducted by Tavaus, the demos are incredibly convincing and make for a grim future for video calls.

As Emad Mostaque [put it](https://x.com/EMostaque/status/2105744708299526243), "remote work is cooked". That might be premature, but imagine getting on a video call with a job candidate, coworker, or someone claiming to be a family member and having no idea whether they're real.

Griffin-Lite is limited to trusted testers for now while Tavus works on safety and disclosure features before a wider release.

The technology is impressive. The potential for scams is equally impressive, unfortunately (good luck trusting video calls in a few years).

Tweet:  (https://twitter.com/AutismCapital/status/2105806982284480684?s=20)


----------

----------
# TRENDING TOOLS


--------------------
* [FLUX 3 Image](https://x.com/bfl_ai/status/2105734605621825738?s=20) - make precise multi-turn edits without changing any other pixel
